title: Choosing exactly the columns you want

steps.title: Fill in the missing word
steps.task: Fill the blank so the query shows prices.
hints: The blank sits right after SELECT.
One word, starts with 'p'.
It's the prices of products.
Replace ___ with price.
steps.memory_trick: Whatever you write after SELECT is what you see.

steps.title: Three columns
steps.prompt:
More columns, same idea - just keep adding commas.
This is called choosing a PROJECTION: you shine a light on only the columns you need.
steps.task: Try typing: SELECT name, price, stock FROM products;
hints: Start from SELECT name, price …
The third column is stock.
Add a comma before the last one.
Write: SELECT name, price, stock FROM products;
steps.expected_sql: SELECT name, price, stock FROM products;
steps.memory_trick: Three columns, two commas. Count them!

steps.title: Fix the broken query
steps.task: Fix the query so it returns both name and price.
hints: Read it aloud: 'SELECT name price' - that sounds joined together.
In a list, what marks the end of one item?
Name and price are two different columns of one list.
Add a comma between name and price.
steps.memory_trick: Columns in a list are joined by commas, like items on a shopping list.

steps.title: The star shortcut
steps.prompt:
Sometimes you do want every column. The * (star) is SQL's shortcut: 'all of them.'
SELECT * means 'every column.' It's the lazy-but-handy choice.
hints: We want every column.
There's a one-character shortcut.
It's the star symbol on your keyboard.
Type: SELECT * FROM products;

steps.title: Predict the output
steps.prompt:
What will SELECT * FROM customers; show you?
(Look at the customers table before you answer.)
steps.task: How many columns does the result have?
hints: Run the query in the Output pane to peek - prediction is fair game.
Count the headings the table has.
name, email, city, and one more.
Answer: 4 columns.
steps.memory_trick: * gives you exactly the same columns as the table.
